## Transactions

A single `SaveChangesAsync` is normally the transaction boundary for one
application operation. Use an explicit transaction when a concrete use case
needs several database operations or several `SaveChangesAsync` calls to succeed
atomically. Do not attempt distributed transactions with EF transaction APIs.

## Compiled Queries

Normal LINQ is the default; EF Core already caches query compilation by query
shape. `EF.CompileQuery`/`EF.CompileAsyncQuery` pay off only on a measured hot
path where profiling shows compilation or cache lookup overhead is material — not
merely because a query runs frequently.

| Scenario | Default technique |
|---|---|
| Read-only entity query | `AsNoTracking()` when useful |
| Read model | Database-side projection |
| Primary-key entity lookup | `FindAsync` when its semantics fit |
| Complex entity graph | Explicit `Include` / projection |
| Set-based mass update/delete | `ExecuteUpdateAsync` / `ExecuteDeleteAsync` when appropriate |
| Normal query | Ordinary LINQ |
| Measured extremely hot query | Consider a compiled query |
| Multiple commits requiring atomicity | Explicit transaction |
| Production schema change | Reviewed migration script, controlled deployment |
| Empty Development database | Run the maintained development seeder |
| Need a fresh local seed dataset | Recreate the local database explicitly |

Hedging issues parallel or delayed duplicate attempts. Use it only for
operations that are safe to execute multiple times — typically idempotent reads
against interchangeable endpoints — never for state-changing operations by
default.

## Database Resilience

Do not wrap normal EF Core operations in a generic application-level retry
pipeline by default. When the provider supports transient retry through EF Core
execution strategies or provider configuration, prefer that mechanism, and
handle transaction/retry interaction according to the provider's EF Core
guidance. An HTTP retry policy is not automatically appropriate for database
operations.

## Message Publishing

Retrying publication can produce duplicate delivery. Use idempotent consumers,
broker-supported deduplication, outbox patterns, or other mechanisms when the
business requirement needs them; a retry policy does not provide exactly-once
delivery.

## Development Seeder Implementation

The seeder assumes the Development schema was already migrated to the current
revision. For a new local database the developer applies the current
migrations first; application startup then populates the empty schema.

### Dataset shape

Cover the main meaningful states and relationships, for example where
applicable: newly created; active or in progress; completed; inactive or
archived; entities with and without optional values; with and without optional
relationships; representative status values; meaningful boundary states. Do not
attempt every combination. When the required entity graph or scenarios are
complex, the task requirements should describe the dataset explicitly rather
than leaving Claude to invent a large generic object graph.

Use one or more representative root/anchor entities to detect existing data.

Authentication determines who the caller is; authorization determines what an
authenticated caller may do. Prefer policies when authorization logic is more
than a trivial role check.

## Choosing Authentication

Choose the scheme from the actual application:

- Bearer/OIDC for an SPA calling an API;
- cookies for server-rendered interactive web applications;
- ASP.NET Core Identity when the application owns local users and passwords;
- an external OpenID Connect/OAuth provider when identity is delegated.

Do not add ASP.NET Core Identity merely because there is a business entity named
`User` or user/profile management; use it when the application owns local
identity accounts and credentials and needs Identity's account management. Do
not issue custom JWTs when an existing identity provider already owns token
issuance.

Add a distributed backend such as Redis only when deployment requirements
justify it.

| Need | Default consideration |
|---|---|
| Entire reusable HTTP response | ASP.NET Core output caching |
| Local application cache | In-memory or HybridCache |
| Multi-instance shared cache | Distributed cache / HybridCache L2 (Reserved: new infrastructure) |
| Expensive repeated remote read | Cache in Infrastructure when the contract permits |
| Application-controlled invalidation | Application abstraction + Infrastructure implementation |
| Unknown performance problem | Measure before adding caching |
